newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coffee market set for Brazil frost roller coaster.
newsitem.headline: Coffee market set for Brazil frost roller coaster.

text.p: With coffee prices at 20-year highs, coffee drinkers are hoping that old man winter stays away from Brazil, the world's biggest producer.

Three years after two severe, sudden frosts hit the country's key growing regions and ignited world coffee prices, a mere whisper of colder weather is enough to fuel futures prices in London and New York.
It is still early to worry about a crop-damaging frost this year, and meteorologists are forecasting no threatening cold in the coming eight days.

"It is going to turn much colder in Argentina next week," said Weather Services Corp. meterologist Mike Palmerino. "Some of the cool air could spill into Brazil, but it's a far cry from having a freeze in Brazil's coffee areas," he said.

"Even though the colder weather next week is not expected to impact the coffee belt, we are getting near to the freeze season and people do not want to be short," said Steve Platt, a market analyst at Dean Witter.
"The market is still responding to tightness," Platt said.
Market reaction to a frost -- as it was in 1994 - is immediate. But the impact of the frost is not on the crop being harvested but on the following year's harvest, in this case that of 1998.
Brazilian farmers are more concerned about a freeze than usual as they are counting on a bumper harvest in 1998 to make up for what is expected to be a smaller crop this year.
The key danger months are June, July and August. A frost was recorded before June only once in the past century.

Marcio Custodio of independent meteorologists Somar, sounded a note of warning that this year winter had begun early, pointing to the low temperatures already being seen in coffee areas such as Pocos de Caldas and April frosts in the far south of the country.
But if winter has started early, it may also finish early, said Francisco Assis, forecaster at Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology (Inmet).
"The cold should continue through June. But in July it should start to get better," Assis said.

Coffee traders are taking no chances. They pushed up the price of coffee futures at the Coffee, Cocoa and Sugar Exchange in New York to a 20-year high on Thursday when the price of the May contract surged to 277.5 cents a pound.
Prices retreated slightly Friday with the May contract dropping 0.55 cents and ending at 276.5 cents a pound.
